title: Tools, Workspace & Safety Setup
html:
The build station

A clean, well-lit, ventilated bench is the single biggest predictor of a clean build. Before you touch a single component, assemble your kit. Buying the right tools once saves you from stripped screws, cold joints, and burned-out FCs.

The non-negotiable tool kit

ToolSpec / why
Soldering ironTemperature-controlled, 60-80W. A TS100/TS101 or Pinecil with a chisel/bevel tip. Avoid 25W pencil irons — they cannot heat fat battery pads.
Solder63/37 leaded rosin-core, 0.7-1.0mm. Leaded flows easier and is more forgiving than lead-free for hobby work.
FluxNo-clean rosin flux (pen or paste). Makes joints wet and shiny.
Hex driversQuality 1.5mm, 2.0mm, 2.5mm drivers. Cheap drivers strip M2/M3 motor screws instantly.
MultimeterContinuity beep + DC volts. Used for short-checks and the smoke test.
Helping hands / viseArticulated arms or a small PCB vise to hold the frame while both hands work.
MiscSide cutters (flush), tweezers, isopropyl alcohol 99%, heat-shrink, zip ties, threadlocker (blue, medium).
Tip.
A silicone heat-resistant mat protects the bench, won't melt under the iron, and the soft surface keeps tiny screws from rolling away.

Ventilation and fume safety

Rosin solder smoke is an irritant and a known respiratory sensitizer. Never breathe it directly. A small fume extractor with an activated-carbon filter placed between your face and the joint, or a fan pulling smoke away toward an open window, is mandatory. Solder in a ventilated space, not a sealed closet.

SAFETY: LiPo handling.
Store and charge LiPos in a fire-safe container (LiPo bag, ammo can, or ceramic pot) away from anything flammable. Never leave a charging pack unattended. A punctured or puffed cell can vent and ignite — keep a Class-D or sand-based extinguisher nearby, not just water. Designate a LiPo location BEFORE you start building.

Workspace layout

  • Lighting — a bright daylight LED lamp plus a magnifier helps you spot bridges and cold joints.
  • ESD — FCs and ESCs are static-sensitive. A grounded mat or touching a grounded surface before handling helps.
  • Organization — magnetic parts tray for screws; label bags from your build kit so nothing walks off.
▸Hands-On

Photograph your build station with every required tool laid out.

  1. Lay out iron, solder, flux, hex drivers, multimeter, cutters, and helping hands on your mat.
  2. Set up and photograph your fume extraction (fan or extractor) showing airflow direction.
  3. Designate and photograph your fire-safe LiPo charge/storage location.
  4. Write a checklist confirming ventilation, ESD precaution, and LiPo safety are in place.

title: Soldering Primer: Flux, Tinning & Good vs Cold Joints
html:
The physics of a joint

Soldering is not gluing. A good joint forms a metallurgical bond where molten solder wets both metal surfaces and forms an alloy at the interface. To wet, both surfaces must be hotter than the solder's melting point and clean of oxides — that is the entire job of flux and tip prep.

Iron setup

  • Temperature — set 320-350°C for small signal pads, 360-380°C for big battery and ESC pads. Hotter is faster, not better; over 400°C burns flux instantly and lifts pads.
  • Tip — use a chisel or bevel tip, never a fine conical, for power pads. More contact area = faster heat transfer.
  • Tinning the tip — keep a small bead of fresh solder on the tip at all times. A dry, blackened tip transfers almost no heat.

Tinning pads and wires

The workflow that makes joints reliable is tin both sides, then join:

  1. Flux the pad. Touch the tip to the pad, feed a little solder until it flows into a small shiny dome. That's a tinned pad.
  2. Twist the wire strands, flux them, and flow solder into the strands until they turn silver. That's a tinned wire.
  3. Hold the tinned wire on the tinned pad, touch the iron to both for ~1-2 seconds. The two pools merge. Remove iron, hold still while it solidifies.
Tip.
The classic order: heat the joint, not the solder. Touch solder to the heated junction so capillary action pulls it in. Dripping solder off the iron onto a cold pad is the #1 cause of cold joints.

Reading the result

JointLooks likeCause
GoodShiny, smooth, slightly concave, wets up the wireBoth sides hot, clean, fluxed
ColdDull, grainy, blobby, ball sitting on topNot enough heat or moved while cooling
BridgedSolder connecting two adjacent padsToo much solder; wick or reflow to clear
Dry/lifted padPad brown or peeled off PCBToo hot, too long
joint-check
GOOD shiny volcano, wire fully wetted COLD dull grey blob, ball on surface BRIDGE two pads joined -> wick + reflux tug-test: wire must not move under gentle pull
SAFETY.
A 350°C iron looks identical hot or cold. Always return it to the stand, never the bench. Wash hands after handling leaded solder; do not eat at the bench.
▸Hands-On

Solder ten practice joints and self-grade each one.

  1. On a protoboard, tin ten pads and tin ten wire ends.
  2. Join each, deliberately making a couple cold (low temp) and one bridge to learn the look.
  3. Tug-test every joint gently — any movement = fail.
  4. Photograph all ten and label each good or cold/bridged with the reason.

title: Planning the Build & Component Layout
html:
Plan before you solder

Once a wire is soldered, moving it means desoldering. Ten minutes of dry-fitting and sketching saves hours of rework and produces a cleaner, lighter, better-balanced quad. The goal of layout is threefold: balance the center of gravity, keep antennas clear and protected, and route wires short and tidy.

The stack

On a typical 5-inch freestyle quad, the electronics live in a 30.5x30.5mm or 20x20mm bolt-pattern stack inside the frame:

  • Bottom: 4-in-1 ESC — sits low and central, motor wires fan out to the arms, battery pads face the rear toward the XT60.
  • Top: Flight Controller (FC) — soft-mounted above the ESC, USB port and bind button accessible, arrow pointing forward (nose).
  • Connections — most 4-in-1 stacks use an 8-pin JST-SH cable between ESC and FC carrying motor signals + battery power.
Tip.
Orient the FC so the printed arrow points to the nose. If the geometry forces another orientation, note the yaw offset (e.g. yaw 90) now — you'll set it in Betaflight later. Decide this BEFORE soldering anything directional.

Component placement decisions

  1. VTX — mount near the rear, away from the GPS and RX, with a clear path for its antenna out the back of the frame. VTX runs hot, give it airflow.
  2. Receiver (RX) — small ELRS/Crossfire RX tucks under the top plate or on a standoff. Keep its antenna away from the VTX antenna and carbon.
  3. Camera — sits in the front cage between the side plates; cable runs back to the FC/VTX.
  4. Capacitor — a low-ESR cap (e.g. 35V 470uF-1000uF) on the battery pads is strongly recommended to absorb voltage spikes — plan a spot for it.

Center of gravity and weight

The battery straps on top or bottom; its position sets the CG. Aim for CG slightly forward of the prop center. Keep heavy items (battery, ESC) central and low. Route the battery lead so the XT60 sits where the pack plugs in naturally without a sharp bend.

top-view layout
NOSE (FC arrow ->) M3 o========[ CAM ]========o M1 | [ FC: arrow^ ] | | [ 4in1 ESC + cap ] | | [ RX ] | M2 o=====[ VTX -> ant ]====o M4 TAIL (vtx antenna exits rear)
SAFETY.
Never let a VTX or RX antenna route across or near a spinning prop disc. A severed antenna mid-flight can mean total signal loss. Plan exit points that clear the props by a wide margin.
▸Hands-On

Dry-fit every component and sketch the final layout.

  1. Place the ESC, FC, RX, VTX, camera, and capacitor into the frame with no soldering.
  2. Confirm the FC arrow orientation and note any yaw offset needed.
  3. Mark wire routes and both antenna exit points on a sketch or annotated photo.
  4. Verify nothing fouls a prop and the CG sits central/slightly forward.

title: Mounting Motors and the 4-in-1 ESC
html:
Mechanical first

Get the mechanical assembly right before any soldering. The two failures here — a screw that pierces a motor winding, or an ESC shorting against carbon — are silent until you power up and let the smoke out.

Screw length: the most important number

Most 5-inch motors use an M3 bolt pattern with a typical screw depth of around 5-6mm into the motor base. The arm thickness plus screw length must not exceed the available depth, or the screw tip presses into the motor's stator windings and shorts a phase.

  • Check the motor spec for max screw depth (often printed or in the listing, e.g. M3 x 6mm max).
  • Measure arm thickness (commonly 3-4mm carbon).
  • Pick screws so: arm thickness + thread engagement ≤ motor max depth. When in doubt, use a shorter screw with a washer.
SAFETY: screws into windings.
Before final tightening, spin each motor by hand after seating the screws. Any scratchy resistance or a screw tip visible inside the bell means the screw is too long — stop and shorten it. A pierced winding will smoke the moment you connect a battery.

Mounting motors

  1. Apply a tiny drop of blue (medium) threadlocker to each screw — vibration backs out untreated screws in minutes. Never use red (permanent).
  2. Seat the motor flat on the arm, start all four screws by hand, then tighten in a cross pattern.
  3. Tighten firmly but not gorilla-tight — M3 in carbon strips easily. Snug, then a quarter turn.
  4. Route each motor's three wires inward along the arm toward the ESC; don't trim to length yet.

Seating the 4-in-1 ESC

The ESC bolts into the frame on standoffs (M3, usually 30.5x30.5mm). The danger is the bottom of the ESC PCB touching the carbon frame or a metal standoff and shorting.

  • Use the supplied nylon standoffs or rubber gummies to lift the ESC off the frame plate.
  • Confirm the bottom of the ESC clears any carbon — add nylon washers if needed.
  • Orient the ESC so the battery pads face the rear (toward where the XT60 exits) and the motor pads are nearest their respective arms.
  • Confirm the stack sits flat and level — a tilted ESC means the FC above it won't seat.
screw-length check
motor max depth ...... 6.0 mm arm thickness ........ 4.0 mm screw length ......... 8.0 mm -> 4mm into stator = SHORT screw length ......... 6.0 mm -> 2mm engage, safe rule: length - arm <= max depth
▸Hands-On

Mount all four motors and the ESC into the frame.

  1. Calculate correct screw length for your motor max depth and arm thickness.
  2. Threadlock and mount all four motors; spin each by hand to confirm no winding contact.
  3. Seat the 4-in-1 ESC on standoffs/gummies with the battery pads facing rear.
  4. Confirm the stack is flat, level, and the ESC bottom clears all carbon.

title: Soldering Motors, ESC & FC Power
html:
Now the soldering

With everything mounted, solder the high-current connections. This is where good iron technique pays off — these pads carry tens of amps, and a cold joint here means dropouts, desyncs, or a fire.

Motor leads to the ESC

Each motor has three wires going to three pads per corner on the 4-in-1 ESC. The order does not matter electrically yet — any of the three can go to any of the three pads, because motor direction is fixed later in software or by swapping any two. So solder them in whatever order routes cleanest.

  1. Trim each motor wire to length so it reaches its corner pads with a gentle, strain-free arc — not bar-tight, not a big loop.
  2. Strip ~2mm, tin the wire ends, and pre-tin the ESC motor pads.
  3. Solder each wire to its pad: heat the joint, the two tinned pools merge, hold still while it sets.
  4. Tug-test each. Keep the three wires from one motor neat and parallel.
Tip.
Don't worry about getting motor direction right by wire order. You'll reverse any motor in BLHeli/Bluejay or by swapping two of its three wires after the build. Solder for tidiness now, set direction in Lesson 2.7.

Battery lead and capacitor

The XT60 pigtail and the low-ESR capacitor both go on the ESC's big battery pads, marked + (or BAT+/VBAT) and - (GND).

  • Use thick wire (typically 14AWG on a 5-inch). Tin both the wire and the fat pads with the iron set hot (~370°C) — these pads sink a lot of heat.
  • Red to +, black to -. Reversing this destroys the ESC and FC instantly.
  • Solder the capacitor across the same pads, observing polarity: the cap's stripe/short leg is negative. Heat-shrink the cap legs to prevent shorts.
SAFETY: verify polarity.
Before ever connecting a battery, set your multimeter to continuity and confirm: battery + traces to BAT+, battery - traces to GND, and NO continuity between + and -. A reversed XT60 or a + to - bridge is the single most common build-killer. Check twice.

FC-to-ESC connection

Most stacks ship with a plug-and-play 8-pin JST-SH harness that carries the four motor signals plus VBAT and GND from ESC to FC. Just plug it in — confirm it's keyed correctly and fully seated. If your stack instead uses solder pads, match each pad label (M1-M4, VBAT, GND, CURR) one-to-one between boards.

polarity verify (DMM continuity)
XT60 red -> ESC BAT+ ... beep XT60 black -> ESC GND ... beep BAT+ <-> GND ............. silent (no short) cap stripe -> GND ....... correct polarity
▸Hands-On

Solder all motor leads and the battery lead to the ESC.

  1. Trim, tin, and solder all twelve motor wires to their corner pads; tug-test each.
  2. Solder the XT60 lead (red=+, black=-) and the capacitor to the battery pads, watching cap polarity.
  3. Plug in or solder the FC-to-ESC harness.
  4. Photograph each joint and visually inspect for cold joints, bridges, or stray strands.

title: Wiring the Receiver, Camera & VTX
html:
Signal wiring

These are the low-current, low-margin-for-error connections. Each device connects to specific FC pads, and getting the UART and voltage right matters. Pull out the port plan you made earlier — that map is your wiring contract.

The receiver (RX)

A serial RX (ELRS, Crossfire, or similar) needs four connections to a free UART:

RX pinFC padNotes
VCC5V (or 4V5)Most modern RX run on 5V — check the module
GNDGNDCommon ground
TX (RX module)FC RX of a UARTCrossed: module TX -> FC RX
RX (RX module)FC TX of the same UARTmodule RX -> FC TX
Tip.
UART pairs are always crossed: the receiver's TX goes to the flight controller's RX. Mixing these up is the most common reason a brand-new RX shows no telemetry or won't bind in software.

The FPV camera

An analog camera typically has three wires: power, ground, and video out.

  • VCC — match the camera's input range. Many run 5V; some accept battery voltage on a dedicated pad. Don't feed 4S/6S into a 5V-only cam.
  • GND — to a GND pad.
  • Video — to the FC's CAM / video-in pad (the FC's OSD overlays here, then passes video to the VTX), or directly to the VTX video-in depending on your stack.

The VTX

The video transmitter usually needs power, ground, video-in, and often a control wire (SmartAudio/IRC Tramp) for changing channels and power from the OSD:

  • VBAT — most VTXs take raw battery voltage (check; some are 5V only). Powering a battery-rated VTX from 5V starves it.
  • GND — common ground.
  • Video in — from the FC video-out pad (so OSD is included).
  • SmartAudio — single wire to a spare UART TX for OSD control. Set the UART to that protocol later.
SAFETY.
Never power up a VTX without an antenna attached. Transmitting into an open connector reflects power back and can permanently burn the VTX amplifier. Confirm the antenna is connected before any power-up in the next lessons.
wiring map (example)
RX: 5V / GND / TX1 / RX1 (UART1, crossed) CAM: 5V / GND / vid-in (FC CAM) VTX: VBAT / GND / vid-out / SmartAudio->TX6 verify each VCC matches device voltage rating
▸Hands-On

Solder the RX, camera, and VTX per your UART map.

  1. Solder the RX to a free UART (remember TX/RX cross) at the correct voltage.
  2. Wire the camera power, ground, and video to the FC.
  3. Wire the VTX power, ground, video-in, and SmartAudio.
  4. Continuity-check each VCC and GND, then build a photo log of every connection labeled with its pad.

title: Antenna Mounting, Props & Setting Motor Direction
html:
Antennas, rotation, props

Three jobs that decide whether the quad flies straight and whether you keep video and control link: mounting antennas with strain relief, setting motor direction, and installing props in the right CW/CCW positions.

Mounting the antennas

  • VTX antenna — route the coax out the rear with no sharp bends (keep bend radius generous; coax kinks ruin SWR). Secure it in a TPU antenna mount or tube so it can't flop into a prop. The radiating tip should be clear of carbon.
  • RX antennas — for diversity RX, mount the two antenna tips at 90 degrees to each other for polarization diversity. Keep the active tip (the exposed coax end) away from carbon, the VTX antenna, and ESC.
  • Strain relief — the weak point is where coax meets the connector/board. Add a service loop and anchor the cable with a zip tie or hot glue so vibration and crashes don't fatigue the joint.
SAFETY.
Re-confirm no antenna can reach the prop disc. A loose VTX antenna sucked into a 5-inch prop at full throttle is both a signal loss and a shrapnel hazard. TPU mounts with a captured tube are the standard fix.

Motor direction

Quad motors spin in a specific pattern. The modern default in Betaflight is props-out (front motors spin outward at the front). The diagonal pairs spin the same direction:

MotorPositionDirection (props-out)
M1Rear-rightCCW
M2Front-rightCW
M3Rear-leftCW
M4Front-leftCCW

You set direction in software (BLHeli_S/Bluejay or BLHeli_32 via the configurator's motor tab, props OFF) or by physically swapping any two of a motor's three wires. Confirm each motor matches the diagram in the Betaflight/ESC motor test before installing props.

Installing props

Props are handed: CW props go on CW motors, CCW props on CCW motors. Self-tightening prop nuts tighten in the direction opposite to motor spin. Props are usually marked, or the leading edge (the higher, smoother edge) faces the direction of rotation.

SAFETY: props off until smoke test passes.
Do NOT install props for power-up testing yet. Lay them in position only. Props go on last, after the smoke test and motor-direction check are both confirmed (next lesson). A quad that arms unexpectedly with props on can cause serious injury.
props-out rotation (top view)
FRONT M4 CCW ) ( CW M2 \ / XX / \ M3 CW ) ( CCW M1 REAR match prop hand to motor direction; nuts self-tighten
▸Hands-On

Mount both antennas and lay out props in correct rotation (not powered).

  1. Mount the VTX and RX antennas with TPU mounts and a strain-relief service loop.
  2. Confirm no antenna can reach the prop disc.
  3. Confirm your intended motor directions (props-out) on the diagram.
  4. Lay the four props in their correct CW/CCW positions and take a labeled photo — do not install or power.

title: The Pre-Flight Smoke Test & Continuity Checks
html:
The moment of truth

The smoke test is the first time the build sees voltage. Done right, a wiring fault reveals itself harmlessly. Done wrong, you watch a $40 stack vaporize. The procedure has two phases: a powered-off continuity check, then a current-limited first power-up — props OFF.

Phase 1: continuity / short check (no power)

Set your multimeter to continuity (beep) mode and verify:

  1. No short across the input. Probe battery + and battery - at the XT60. It should be SILENT (the cap may cause a brief charge-up beep then silence). A solid beep = a dead short; do not connect a battery.
  2. Polarity continuity. XT60 + traces to BAT+/VBAT pads; XT60 - traces to GND. Both should beep.
  3. No signal-pad shorts. Spot-check that 5V does not beep to GND, and VBAT does not beep to GND.
SAFETY: find the short FIRST.
If + to - beeps, STOP. Inspect for solder bridges on the battery pads, a reversed capacitor, a stray wire whisker, or a pierced motor winding. Never apply battery power to a shorted board — that is exactly what releases the smoke.

Phase 2: smoke-stopper power-up (props off)

A smoke-stopper is an inline device with a low-wattage incandescent bulb (or a current-limited supply) between battery and quad. If there's a short, the bulb glows bright and limits current to a safe trickle instead of dumping the full LiPo into the fault.

  1. Remove all props (confirm — props OFF).
  2. Connect the quad through the smoke-stopper to a battery (or use a bench supply set to a low current limit, e.g. 1A).
  3. Watch and smell. The bulb should flash briefly (cap inrush) then go dim/dark. A bulb that stays bright = a short still present — disconnect immediately.
  4. Confirm the FC, ESC, VTX, and RX LEDs come alive. No component should get hot. No smoke, no smell.
  5. Plug in USB and confirm the FC enumerates in the configurator; check the motor tab shows correct motor mapping and direction (still props off).
Tip.
No smoke-stopper? Use a bench power supply with a current limit set low (~0.5-1A) for the first power-up — it does the same job. Touch each chip with a fingertip after a few seconds; anything hot signals a fault.
smoke-test log
continuity + to - ........ no short polarity + ->BAT+ ........ beep ok smoke-stopper power ...... flash then dim FC / ESC / VTX / RX LED .. all alive component temps .......... cool motor tab direction ...... verify props off
SAFETY.
If anything smokes, smells, or gets hot, disconnect the battery instantly and move the LiPo to your fire-safe location. Do not re-power until you have found and fixed the fault.
▸Hands-On

Run a short-check then a first power-up and log the results.

  1. Continuity-check + to - (no short) and confirm polarity to the pads.
  2. Confirm all props are OFF.
  3. Power up through a smoke-stopper or current-limited supply; watch for flash-then-dim and any smoke or heat.
  4. Confirm all device LEDs, check temps, and log each result as pass/fail.

title: Cable Management, Soft-Mounting & Final Airframe
html:
Finishing the airframe

A quad that passed the smoke test still isn't flight-ready. Loose wires get cut by props or fatigue and break; a hard-mounted FC picks up motor vibration that corrupts the gyro and causes oscillations. The final pass is cable management, soft-mounting, and a mechanical sign-off.

Cable management

  • Service loops, not tension. Every wire should have a gentle loop so a crash flexes the wire, not the solder joint. Bar-tight wires rip pads off.
  • Anchor everything. Use small zip ties or a dab of hot glue to secure wire runs to standoffs and the frame. Trim zip-tie tails flush.
  • Clear the prop arc. Tuck all wiring and antennas inside the frame's protected zone. Nothing should overhang where a prop spins.
  • Strain-relieve the battery lead and antennas. These take the most abuse. A loop of wire anchored before the connector saves the joint.
  • Reinforce solder joints. A drop of hot glue over signal-wire joints (RX, cam, VTX, capacitor legs) prevents vibration cracking and accidental shorts.

Soft-mounting the FC

The gyro must read airframe motion, not high-frequency motor buzz. Soft-mounting isolates it:

  • Rubber gummies / grommets — the FC sits on silicone grommets pressed onto the standoffs, with M3 screws passing through. The FC floats on rubber, not rigid metal.
  • Don't over-tighten — crushing the gummies defeats the isolation. The FC should be slightly compliant, not clamped solid.
  • Ensure the soft-mounted FC still can't shift enough to short against the ESC or standoffs.
Tip.
Good soft-mounting reduces gyro noise and lets you run less filtering in Betaflight, which improves response and reduces latency. A hard-mounted FC is a leading cause of hot motors and the dreaded mid-throttle oscillation.

Final mechanical sign-off

Before the quad is declared flight-ready, walk a checklist:

CheckPass criteria
Motor screwsThreadlocked, tight, no winding contact
Prop nutsCorrect hand, will self-tighten (props installed LAST)
WiringService loops, anchored, clear of prop arc
FC soft-mountOn gummies, compliant, can't short
AntennasStrain-relieved, clear of props, connected
Smoke testPassed, no heat/smoke
SAFETY.
Install props only after all checks pass and only when you are ready to fly with a clear failsafe configured. Before the first flight, confirm in software that throttle-cut/failsafe drops the motors when the link is lost, and always remove the battery before working on the quad. Verify current FAA and local rules for registration and flying location before any outdoor flight.
▸Hands-On

Finish cable management and soft-mounting, then sign off the build.

  1. Anchor and strain-relieve every wire and antenna; reinforce signal joints with hot glue.
  2. Soft-mount the FC on gummies without over-tightening.
  3. Confirm nothing fouls the prop arc and the FC can't short.
  4. Complete the mechanical sign-off checklist confirming the quad is flight-ready (props installed last, before flight).
